Ministerial Staff
-----------------

Meet our team of Second-Ponce ministers.

**Minister of Music**

Bill Gabbard has been a professional vocal musician for over thirty-eight years, the last thirty-one with The Soldiers’ Chorus of The United States Army Field Band of Washington, D.C.

Bill served his local church in Annapolis, Maryland, as a church officer, worship committee chair and adult choir director. For ten years, he has performed with “Brethren,” an acclaimed Washington, D.C-based men’s choral group.

Bill’s wife, Mary Lynn, is a proud native of Atlanta. They met in college at Mercer University where they were both members of the Mercer Singers. They are the parents of five and grateful grandparents of six. Their two oldest sons are currently serving as commissioned officers in the Navy and Army.

![Image 1](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/611fbf22e15d6f23b9db1a6e/bb343c62-5b21-4881-a026-7c959a588371/IMG_3543.jpg)

### Bill Gabbard

**Minister of Community and Student Discipleship**

Jonathan Hall is a graduate of Mercer University’s McAfee School of Theology in Atlanta. Before joining Second-Ponce, he served with the youth and music ministries at Smoke Rise Baptist Church in Stone Mountain, Georgia. Jonathan also has worked as staff for Passport Camps. Originally from North Carolina, Jonathan completed his undergraduate degree at Wofford College in Spartanburg, South Carolina. When he is not spending time with his wife, Milligan—perhaps enjoying a meal together at one of Atlanta’s many delicious restaurants--you can find Jonathan listening to records from his collection, playing basketball with friends or making all kinds of art.

![Image 2](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/611fbf22e15d6f23b9db1a6e/25703aa2-55fc-4724-84d3-bb79c4a90b7b/Jonathan+Hall+Staff+Pic.jpg)

### Rev. Jonathan Hall

**Minister of Missions and Children’s Discipleship**

Allie Osborne is from Richmond, Va. and moved to Atlanta in 2021 with her two cats, Poppy and Scooter. She has lived and worked in the Cooperative Baptist tradition her entire life, serving in both children’s and youth ministry positions. Allie has an undergraduate degree in Communication from Christopher Newport University in Virginia and a Masters of Divinity from McAfee School of Theology at Mercer University here in Atlanta. Her favorite activities are reading, hiking and enjoying Mexican food.

![Image 3](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/611fbf22e15d6f23b9db1a6e/245c1017-3497-40bc-a548-67e346df437d/IMG_3519.jpg)

### Rev. Allie Osborne

**Carl Edward Sanders Sr.** (May 15, 1925 – November 16, 2014) was an American lawyer and politician who served as the 74th [governor of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Georgia "Governor of Georgia") from 1963 to 1967.

Early life and education
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Sanders&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\]

Carl Sanders was born on May 15, 1925, in [Augusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta,_Georgia "Augusta, Georgia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_/(U.S._state/) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), United States to a middle class family. He later stated that he had "an exceptionally happy and secure childhood."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988169%E2%80%93170-1) He attended the [Academy of Richmond County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Richmond_County "Academy of Richmond County"), where he performed well academically and played on the school [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") team. He was made an alternate appointee to the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy"), but when the primary appointee claimed the spot Sanders accepted a football scholarship and enrolled at the [University of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Georgia "University of Georgia")[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988170-2) in 1942. He played as a left-handed [quarterback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarterback "Quarterback") on the freshman football team.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3)

While Sanders was at college, the United States entered World War II, and in 1943 he left his studies and joined the [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces"). He was commissioned as a lieutenant and piloted [B-17 Flying Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-17_Flying_Fortress "B-17 Flying Fortress") aircraft.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988170-2) He named his own bomber "Georgia Peach", but was never deployed overseas.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) After the war he returned to the University of Georgia to complete his studies. He studied law, passing the bar examination in early 1947 and finishing his courses in December. He played with the [Georgia Bulldogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Bulldogs_football "Georgia Bulldogs football") and went to the [Oil Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_Bowl "Oil Bowl"). He was a member of the [Chi Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi_Phi "Chi Phi") fraternity, the [Phi Kappa Literary Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Kappa_Literary_Society "Phi Kappa Literary Society"), and the school debate team. On September 6, 1947, he married Betty Foy, an art student he had met at the university.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988170-2) They had two children together.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) Sanders started practicing law in Augusta with Henry Hammond before establishing his own practice with several other partners. He devoted a significant amount of time to practice early on to pay off medical debt after his wife fell ill.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988170%E2%80%93171-4)

Sanders garnered an interest in politics from his father, who had served on the Richmond County Board of Commissioners. In 1954, Sanders won a seat in the [Georgia House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_House_of_Representatives "Georgia House of Representatives"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) successfully defeating a "[Cracker Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_cracker "Georgia cracker")" candidate.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) Two years later he was elected to the [Georgia State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_State_Senate "Georgia State Senate"). At the time, a rotation agreement meant the seat was typically held in successive fashion by a denizen of Richmond County, of [Jefferson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_Georgia "Jefferson County, Georgia"), and of [Glascock County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glascock_County,_Georgia "Glascock County, Georgia"). He was re-elected in 1958 and 1960, making him the only person to ever serve three consecutive terms from a multi-county Georgia senatorial constituency while the rotation agreements were in use.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5)

In 1958 Sanders chaired a Senate committee which investigated potential corruption in the Rural Roads Authority during [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Georgia "Governor of Georgia") [Marvin Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Griffin "Marvin Griffin")'s tenure.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson200869-6)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) The committee found that the authority spent too much money on construction projects, located new roads without proper consideration, and was ineffective at maintaining existing roads. It recommended that the agency be dissolved and that future rural road projects be allocated based on population density, all financed with a [pay-as-you-go system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PAYGO "PAYGO").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson200869-6) [Lieutenant Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Georgia "Lieutenant Governor of Georgia") [Ernest Vandiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Vandiver "Ernest Vandiver") became political allies with Sanders as a result of his committee work[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) and made him Senate [floor leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_leader "Floor leader") in 1959.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) Vandiver became governor, and that year a federal judge ordered the [Atlanta Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Board_of_Education "Atlanta Board of Education") to draft a plan to racially desegregate schools. Vandiver called 60 people to the [Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Governor%27s_Mansion "Georgia Governor's Mansion") to discuss either proceeding with desegregation or [closing the schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massive_resistance "Massive resistance"). Only Sanders and House floor leader Frank Twitty advised desegregation, the former fearing that suspending schools "would have created a generation of illiterates."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) Vandiver ultimately had schools closed only temporarily while the [Georgia General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_General_Assembly "Georgia General Assembly") revised state segregation statutes.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) He opposed a proposal to make the school issue subject to a statewide referendum.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson2008113-7) With the governor's support, Sanders was elected president [pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_tempore "Pro tempore") of the Senate on February 20, 1959, after [Robert H. Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_H._Jordan "Robert H. Jordan")'s resignation, and served in that position during the chamber's 1960 and 1962 regular sessions.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-8)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson200894%E2%80%9395-9)

Gubernatorial career
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Sanders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Gubernatorial career")\]

Sanders decided to make a bid for higher office in 1962.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) Initially mulling over a potential race for the office of lieutenant governor which had a retiring incumbent, he had doubts when a similarly-named Atlanta attorney, Carl F. Sanders, declared his candidacy. Carl E. Sanders suspected that the other man had been planted to confuse voters and spoil his chances by another candidate, [Peter Zack Geer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Zack_Geer "Peter Zack Geer"). Geer denied the allegation. Carl E. Sanders then decided to run for governor. At the time he launched his candidacy in late April,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011224-10) Georgia used the [county unit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_unit_system "County unit system") in its primaries, whereby the candidate who won the majority in most counties secured the party nomination, instead of the candidate which earned the majority of all votes across the state. This system greatly limited the chances of urban candidates for decades. Several weeks into the primary, federal courts declared this method unconstitutional, and left the nomination to be decided by popular vote.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) Sanders campaigned on "a platform of progress", pledging to improve education, reorganize the [State Highway Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Department_of_Transportation "Georgia Department of Transportation"), revamp mental health and penal institutions, recruit industry, and [reapportion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apportionment_/(politics/) "Apportionment (politics)") the General Assembly.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988173-11)

Already seeking the nomination in the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_/(United_States/) "Democratic Party (United States)") primary were former governor Marvin Griffin and incumbent Lieutenant Governor [Garland T. Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garland_T._Byrd "Garland T. Byrd"). Byrd withdrew from the race after suffering a heart attack in May.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenderson2008170-12) Griffin was a staunch supporter of [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation "Racial segregation").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) He attacked Sanders as too young for the governorship and not committed enough to defending segregation.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011232-13) Sanders supported segregation but felt it was useless to oppose federal integration orders.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-cookNG-14) He promised to "maintain Georgia's traditional separation"[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988171-5) but said he opposed race-baiting politics and that "I tip my hat to the past, but I take off my coat to the future."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011230-15) He also promised to keep public schools open, even if the federal government ordered them to integrate.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002151-16) Griffin held a rally with Alabama governor-elect [George Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wallace "George Wallace"), another staunch segregationist, to demonstrate his support for racial separation. Sanders mocked this strategy at his own rally the same day, describing Griffin as "so weak in his belief in Georgia and her people that he plans to import an outsider to meddle in our affairs. I don't need an Alabama crutch to help me."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011230-15) Griffin pledged to oppose federal court orders to integrate and throughout the campaign vilified the "Negro bloc vote" in Georgia.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011230-15) Following a confrontation between the white supremacist [Ku Klux Klan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan") and the [Georgia State Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_State_Patrol "Georgia State Patrol") at a Klan rally, Griffin offered that he was unsure of how to handle such a situation. Sanders accused the former governor of having prior knowledge of the rally and of bringing Klansmen into Georgia. Sanders also accused Griffin of having run a corrupt administration in his previous term.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuchanan2011232-13) In the primary, he defeated Griffin, receiving 494,978 votes (58.7 percent) to Griffin's 332,746 (39 percent).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-17) Most of his support came from urban areas.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988173-11) He then won [the general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Georgia_gubernatorial_election "1962 Georgia gubernatorial election").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) He took the oath of office on January 14 and was formally inaugurated as governor the following day.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-18) Aged 37 upon his assumption of the office, he was the youngest governor in the country at the time.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-yardley-19)

Sanders appointed a Governor's Commission for Efficiency and Improvement in Government, which managed reforms in the penal system, mental healthcare, the civil service, the Highway Department, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Education.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202125-20) He worked with Atlanta Mayor [Ivan Allen Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Allen_Jr. "Ivan Allen Jr.") to bring [professional sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_sports "Professional sports") teams to the capital city,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-cookNG-14) and in 1963 he recruited a friend, [Rankin M. Smith Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankin_M._Smith_Sr. "Rankin M. Smith Sr."), to fund the creation of the [Atlanta Falcons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Falcons "Atlanta Falcons") football team.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3)

Sanders campaigned as a racial segregationist and did not actively support the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement") for blacks when in office, but was forced to address racial issues on several occasions. He was regarded by observers as a racial moderate, and described his own position as "a segregationist but not a damned fool."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179-21) He regarded both white reactionaries and black civil rights activists as politically extreme.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179%E2%80%93180-22) Concerned that racial violence would interfere with his plans to expand Georgia's economy, he said, "while I am governor we are going to obey the laws, we are not going to resist federal court orders with violence, and we are not going to close any schools."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179-21) He appointed some blacks to state boards and the first blacks to the State Patrol and [Georgia National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_National_Guard "Georgia National Guard"). Overall, his administration was staffed predominantly by whites and he appointed no black agency heads or judges. When confrontations between different groups over racial issues appeared, he tended to try and negotiate compromises, though he sent state police to Savannah in July 1963 to head off violence and placed police on standby in Atlanta in mid-1966 when Mayor Allen confronted angry black demonstrators.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179-21) He criticized rioters and testified to Congress against the passage of the [Civil Rights Act of 1964](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964"), arguing it violated property rights.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988180-23)

### Legislative affairs

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Sanders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legislative affairs")\]

By the time Sanders became governor, it was common for this official to wield wide influence over the General Assembly, including being able to essentially name the [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_speakers_of_the_Georgia_House_of_Representatives "List of speakers of the Georgia House of Representatives") and legislative committee chairmen. He was one of the last governors to be able to exercise this amount of authority over the legislature.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202126-24)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-galloway-25) In 1963 [Leroy Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leroy_Johnson_/(Georgia_politician/) "Leroy Johnson (Georgia politician)") became the first black state senator in Georgia in decades. When guards at the State Capitol informed Sanders that Johnson and his black pages were ignoring signs designating "white" and "colored" restrooms and water fountains, the governor had the signage removed. Later, Johnson attempted to dine at the Commerce Club, an Atlanta venue frequented by legislators and other members of the state's political and economic elite. The white [maître d'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma%C3%AEtre_d%27 "Maître d'") refused Johnson service, so he contacted Sanders. Sanders called club founder [Robert W. Woodruff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_W._Woodruff "Robert W. Woodruff"), who subsequently instructed the maître d' to serve Johnson.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-galloway-25)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Carl_Sanders_at_podium.jpg/250px-Carl_Sanders_at_podium.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Sanders_at_podium.jpg)

Sanders speaking at an airport dedication, 1966

Sanders was a [fiscal conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiscal_conservative "Fiscal conservative"). Most of his budgeting focus was directed at public education. His administration's 1963 budget recommendation to the General Assembly devoted 56 percent of expenditures to education.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202125-20) At the governor's request, the legislature created the Governor's Commission to Improve Education, with 25 members appointed by the governor.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988174-26) The body included the first black people appointed to a state commission since the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-27)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179-21) Equipped with the commission's recommendations, the following year he stated that Georgia's education system was a "modern crisis" and called for a $30 million increase in taxes to improve schools.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988174-26) This included a 50 cent increase on the tax per gallon on [liquor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquor "Liquor"), a 12 cent increase on the tax per case of beer, 1% increase in the [corporate income tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_income_tax "Corporate income tax"), and the elimination of the vendors' commission on collection of the [general sales tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_sales_tax "General sales tax").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202125-20) He further requested that the [State Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Board_of_Education "Georgia Board of Education") be empowered to establish minimum standards and that $100 million in bonds be issued to fund new educational institution construction. The General Assembly incorporated his suggestions with minimal alterations.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988174-26) Over the course of his tenure, schoolteacher and university faculty salaries were raised,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202125-20) 10,000 additional teachers were hired, a record number of new schools were built, new [junior colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_college "Junior college") and vocational schools were created, and a Governor's Honors Program was established.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988174-26)

Sanders asked the legislature to appropriate funds for airport construction to attract industry to outlying communities. As a result, 33 new community airports were established in Georgia between 1965 and 1966.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-28) Georgia's economy performed well during his tenure, and the state had a budget surplus when he left office.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTELauth202125%E2%80%9326-29)

While serving as governor, Sanders supported an attempt by the General Assembly to draft a new state constitution in 1963.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988176%E2%80%93177-30) The proposed document was prevented from being scheduled for a referendum necessary to ratify it by a [United States district court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_district_court "United States district court"), which ruled that since the legislators who had created the constitution were from malapportioned districts, their work was invalid. Sanders was deeply disappointed by the ruling. The decision was later reversed by the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court "United States Supreme Court"), but by then there was not sufficient political will to revamp the constitution. On February 17, 1964, the Supreme Court ruled in _[Wesberry v. Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesberry_v._Sanders "Wesberry v. Sanders")_ that Georgia had to redraw its [congressional districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_district "Congressional district") to comply with the principle of [one man, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_man,_one_vote "One man, one vote"). The General Assembly had only four days to respond before its session was scheduled for adjournment, but Sanders urged it to redraw the districts. The legislators struggled with the process, and after his own floor leader had resigned the revisions to failure, Sanders visited the House floor on February 21 to encourage the body to keep working. Despite the vocal dissatisfaction of some legislators, a revised districting plan was ultimately passed.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988177-31)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/President_John_F._Kennedy_and_Carl_Sanders.jpg/250px-President_John_F._Kennedy_and_Carl_Sanders.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_John_F._Kennedy_and_Carl_Sanders.jpg)

Sanders with [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") in 1962

Shortly after winning election, Sanders visited President of the United States [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"). He was generally supportive of the president's administration and used his [New Frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Frontier "New Frontier") rhetoric.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988173-11)

In 1964 Sanders appointed a biracial delegation to represent Georgia at the [1964 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Democratic_National_Convention "1964 Democratic National Convention"), the first time that black people were represented on the delegation.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTECook1988179-21) Sanders explained, "\[T\]his is not a social club. This is purely a political organization, based on the fact that every voter should be represented."[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-32)

Under the [term limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit "Term limit") law then in effect, Sanders was ineligible to run for re-election in 1966.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002151-16) In the [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Georgia_gubernatorial_election "1966 Georgia gubernatorial election") campaign that year, he endorsed Democratic nominee [Lester Maddox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Maddox "Lester Maddox"), a segregationist, as his successor though the two had disagreed on many issues. At the Democratic State Convention in [Macon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macon,_Georgia "Macon, Georgia") on October 15, 1966, Sanders told the delegates: "A man should be loyal to his country, his family, to his God and to his political party—and don't you ever forget it."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHathorn198742-33) In his speech, Sanders likened Maddox's [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_/(United_States/) "Republican Party (United States)") opponent, [U.S. Representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Representative "U.S. Representative") [Howard Callaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Callaway "Howard Callaway"), to the "arrogance of [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon"), the chameleon ability of [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") to switch rather than fight, and the callous concern for human needs that is a throwback to [McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley"), [Harding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Harding "Warren G. Harding"), and [Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge "Calvin Coolidge")."[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHathorn198742-33) Callaway criticized Sanders for mishandling the state budget surplus, a position which weakened the Republican among anti-Maddox moderate voters.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHathorn198742-33) Callaway led Maddox in the popular vote but failed to win a majority, and the Democratic-controlled Georgia General Assembly chose Maddox as governor.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Sanders was succeeded by Maddox on January 10, 1967.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-34)

1970 gubernatorial campaign
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Sanders&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1970 gubernatorial campaign")\]

Sanders left office at the peak of his popularity and turned down several offers for federal government positions from President Johnson. Instead he returned to mount an unsuccessful campaign for governor in 1970.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-torpy-35) The other two candidates in the Democratic primary were former state senator [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") and black attorney [Chevene Bowers King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevene_Bowers_King "Chevene Bowers King").[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992613%E2%80%93614,_618-36) Sanders was initially favored by most political observers as the candidate most likely to win.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992616-37) Early polls conducted at the behest of Carter showed most Georgians held a favorable view of Sanders' previous gubernatorial term. Carter directed his campaign team to frame his opponent as anti-democratic, "[nouveau riche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouveau_riche "Nouveau riche")", "Atlanta-oriented", overly liberal, and hostile to George Wallace.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992617,_619-38)

Carter attempted to portray himself as friendly to the "average man" and working-class voters, while portraying Sanders as out-of-touch and regularly referring to him as "[Cuff Links](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cufflink "Cufflink") Carl".[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992624%E2%80%93625-39) He also regularly claimed without basis that Sanders had used his time in office to enrich himself.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992625-40) Sanders ran with the slogan "Carl Sanders ought to be governor again," which appeared to some voters as arrogant.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992624%E2%80%93625-39) Furthermore, while his television advertisements showed him as a man of success while jogging, boating, and flying, Carter's ads focused on his farming background and suggested that Sanders was the candidate of the "big-money boys".[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002159%E2%80%93160-41)

Carter's campaign anonymously distributed a photo of Sanders getting doused with a bottle of champagne by a black [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") basketball player celebrating a victory at a game. The photo communicated several potentially damaging messages about Sanders, including his wealth, an association with alcohol (which was disliked in [teetotalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotalist "Teetotalist") rural communities) and a personal connection with a black person.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002161%E2%80%93162-42) The Carter campaign also published anonymous "fact-sheets" which described Sanders as a staunch ally of controversial black legislator [Julian Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Bond "Julian Bond") (the two actually disliked one another), noted his attendance at the funeral of civil rights activist [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), and attacked him for denying Wallace an official visit to the state. At the same time, the campaign set up a fictitious "Black Concern Committee" to draw black support away from Sanders by arguing that he had failed to honor promises to the black community during his gubernatorial tenure.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002161-43) Carter's campaign press secretary later described their efforts as a "nigger campaign".[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002164-44)

In the September 9 Democratic primary, Carter led with 388,280 votes, while Sanders placed second with 301,179 votes, most of them from blacks or urbanites. With the contest moving to a runoff since no candidate had won an outright majority, Sanders began a series of attacks on Carter. At a press conference shortly after the first primary, he called Carter "a smiling hypocrite" and a staunch liberal.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002164-44) When Carter refused to debate him, Sanders hosted a televised [debate with an empty chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_chair_debating "Empty chair debating"), though the absent opponent brushed the event aside, quipping "Some folks said the chair was ahead."[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002164%E2%80%93165-45) After Carter secured the endorsement of segregationist publisher [Roy V. Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_V._Harris "Roy V. Harris"), Sanders' campaign crafted a pamphlet which depicted Carter climbing into a bed with Harris. Sanders' workers also created another pamphlet showing a picture of dilapidated tenant housing on Carter's farm, captioned "Isn't it time someone spoke up for these people?"[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002165-46) Carter denounced the literature as smear sheets and warned his campaign workers about their distribution. During the last few days of the campaign, Sanders' organization launched an intense effort to fly the pamphlets into far-flung areas of the state. Many were intercepted by Carter supporters posing as Sanders campaigners and destroyed.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002165-46)

In the runoff primary Carter won with 60 percent of the vote. Sanders received 93 percent of the black vote and the support of his erstwhile backers, but Carter won overwhelmingly in rural areas.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002165-46) He felt guilty about the tactics he had employed, and after his win he called Sanders to apologize for attacking his character.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders2002168-47) Carter was victorious in the subsequent general election, and was later elected President of the United States in 1976. Sanders remained bitter about the 1970 campaign, and later said of Carter, "He is not proud of that election, and he shouldn't be proud of it,"[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) though he also thought Carter made "more of a class distinction than a race distinction" in the campaign.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-FOOTNOTESanders1992616-37) He never pursued public office after his loss but remained an active fundraiser for Democratic candidates.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-cookNG-14) He served as the finance chairman of the [Georgia Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Democratic_Party "Georgia Democratic Party") during [George Busbee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Busbee "George Busbee")'s gubernatorial tenure.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-papers-48)

Later life and death
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Sanders&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Later life and death")\]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/20-20-926-sanders.jpg/250px-20-20-926-sanders.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20-20-926-sanders.jpg)

Plaque of Sanders at the [Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Aviation_Hall_of_Fame "Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame")

In 1967 Sanders joined with several other lawyers to create the firm [Troutman, Sanders, Lockerman & Ashmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troutman_Sanders_LLP "Troutman Sanders LLP")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) in Atlanta.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-cookNG-14) He renewed his focus on the firm—which was renamed Troutman Sanders in 1992—after his loss in the 1970 gubernatorial race and recruited [Georgia Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Power "Georgia Power") and [Southern Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Company "Southern Company") as clients. He became chairman of First Georgia Bank in 1973. He served as chairman of the law firm for thirty years, and in 2006 became its chairman emeritus. At the time of his death, Troutman Sanders had grown to include 600 lawyers.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-davis-3) Sanders died in Atlanta on November 16, 2014, at the age of 89, after a fall at his home.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-49)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-yardley-19)

In recognition of his role in encouraging the construction and expansion of airports in Georgia, he was inducted into the [Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Aviation_Hall_of_Fame "Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame") in 1997.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-51) The Carl E. Sanders Family [YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YMCA "YMCA") opened in [Buckhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckhead "Buckhead"), Atlanta, in 2000, after a gift to construct it was made in Sanders’ honor by [Guy Millner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Millner "Guy Millner").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sanders#cite_note-53)

[Dr. James Neil (Dock) Hollingsworth](https://www.bigcanoechapel.com/about/dockhollingsworth.html#)
===================================================================================================

Senior Pastor

[![Image 2](https://www.bigcanoechapel.com/images/staff/dockmore.jpg)](https://www.bigcanoechapel.com/about/dockhollingsworth.html#)

Please welcome Dr. James Neil (Dock) Hollingsworth to Big Canoe Chapel.

Dr. Hollingsworth has been unanimously recommended by the Board of Trustees and the Search Committee to become the next Senior Chaplain for Big Canoe Chapel. The members of Big Canoe Chapel overwhelmingly voted to call Dock to the Chapel. We are excited for him to begin his ministry here in August.

Dock has served as Senior Pastor for Second Ponce De Leon Baptist Church in Atlanta since 2013. He received his BA from Mercer University; his Master of Divinity from Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary; and his Doctor of Ministry from McAfee School of Theology. He has also served as Assistant Dean and Director of Admissions at McAfee School of Theology.

Dock’s numerous interviews received praise from both the 2022 Search Committee and the 2024 Search Committee. Both committees spent many hours watching his Bible based preaching online and visiting his church. We are so pleased that he feels the Lord calling him and his wife, Melissa, to Big Canoe Chapel. He has told us, “I want to be the pastor for all of Big Canoe, as well as the Chapel.”

Dock and Melissa are parents to adult twins, Haley and Brendan. Haley and her husband, Chris Clement are parents to Dock’s “nearly perfect” grandchildren, Cooper and Lucy. Their son, Brendan recently married to Megan, lives in Woodstock. In addition to his love for being a pastor, Dock enjoys golf. Melissa is a retired elementary school teacher and enjoys pickleball.

Let’s give Dock and Melissa a warm welcome from our Big Canoe Chapel family.

He served from 1963 until 1967 as Georgia’s 74th Governor.

Born in Augusta on May 15, 1925, Sanders excelled in athletics at the Academy of Richmond County, where he later was named to the school’s Hall of Fame. After graduation, he attended the University of Georgia on a football scholarship. World War II interrupted his studies, and he enlisted in the Army Air Corps in 1943. At age nineteen he was commissioned to pilot B-17 heavy bombers. After the war he completed his degree and entered the University of Georgia Law School. In 1947, he received his LL.B. degree, was admitted to the bar, and married Betty Bird Foy, a campus beauty, and a talented art student from Statesboro. They settled in Augusta, where their two children, Betty Foy and Carl Edward, Jr., were born.

While practicing law in Augusta, Sanders was active in civic and community affairs and served as a deacon and Sunday school teacher at Hill Baptist Church. In 1955, the Augusta Chamber of Commerce elected him Young Man of the Year, and in 1959 the Georgia Jaycees named him one of the five Outstanding Young Georgians.

Sanders' political career began in 1954 when he was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives, and two years later he advanced to the State Senate, where he was elected President Pro Tempore. In 1962, Sanders ran for Governor, and in a hard-fought campaign, defeated Marvin Griffin, a former governor. Sanders’ victory over Griffin marked a turning point in Georgia's political history. Following the demise of the county unit system, Sanders was the first Georgia governor chosen by popular vote, the first from an urban area to be elected since 1916, and, at age 37, the youngest governor in the country.

In his biography of Sanders, James F. Cook characterized him as the Spokesman of the New South, based upon Governor Sanders’ image as a progressive governor during the turbulent period of the 1960’s, and his strong political advocacy for keeping Georgia’s public schools open when many southern leaders favored closing schools to avoid implementing court orders to desegregate. Although he lived and came of age in a rigidly segregated society, Sanders developed a moderate position on race issues in contrast to a number of other Southern Governors of that period. He befriended and worked with Leroy Johnson, the first African-American to serve in the Georgia Senate, and worked quietly to remove vestiges of the Jim Crow system from the State Capitol and other state facilities. He appointed the first African Americans to serve in the Georgia State Patrol, to the Governor's Commission to Improve Education and to the Georgia delegation to the Democratic National Convention.

Sanders made education the first priority of his administration and directed nearly sixty cents of every tax dollar into education. His administration added 10,000 new teachers, established a Master Plan for Education, and set minimum standards for public schools. In addition, he began the Governor's Honors program for exceptional students, developed an extensive educational television network, encouraged school consolidation, and greatly expanded vocational training.

Within the University System, enrollments doubled during Sanders’ administration. The state’s modest system of community colleges, then known as Junior Colleges, was expanded with the addition of colleges in Brunswick, Albany, Kennesaw, Dalton and Gainesville, Georgia and in Clayton, Bibb and Floyd Counties. Several of these community colleges established under Sanders’ leadership have grown into major colleges within the University System. Specifically, the Georgia Medical College was expanded with the addition of a dental school. Additionally, during his tenure, University System salaries increased by 32 per cent, moving Georgia from tenth to fourth among Southern states. With the support and inspiration of his wife, Betty, who is an accomplished artist, Sanders established the first Georgia Council of the Arts and Humanities, and was responsible for the addition of 4 new fine arts buildings on Georgia college campuses. Governor Sanders later served as President of the University of Georgia Alumni Society and received the Bill Hartman award, which honors former student athletes at the University.

Sanders was instrumental in funding the construction of new and enlarged facilities for the University of Georgia School of Law. Today the Law School offers students a popular leadership program known as the Sanders Leadership Forum, which brings state and national political leaders to the campus.

The Sanders administration also reorganized the State Highway Department, the Welfare Department, and the Health Department; it also built the current Governor’s mansion and established the State Water Quality Control Board as the state’s first environmental regulatory agency and created a police academy. Under Sanders’ leadership, his administration also had the top-ranked airport development program in the nation, with 42 airports being built during Sanders’ term. At the end of his term, Sanders left $140 million in the State treasury--the largest amount ever left to a succeeding governor up to that time.

Governor Sanders served as Chairman of the Southern Governors Conference and, after leaving office, continued as the Conference’s legal counsel and argued a landmark case in the United States Supreme Court that struck down the last vestiges of freight rate discrimination that had hampered industrial growth in the South.

As Governor, he also worked with Atlanta Mayor Ivan Allen to bring professional baseball and football to Atlanta (the Atlanta Braves and Atlanta Falcons). And, after leaving the Governor’s office, Sanders assisted Atlanta developer Tom Cousins in bringing professional basketball to Atlanta (the Atlanta Hawks).

Shortly after his election as governor, Sanders made a successful personal appeal to President John Kennedy to reject a Pentagon recommendation that would have drastically reduced the mission of Augusta’s Fort Gordon. During his tenure as Governor, Sanders also developed a close political and personal friendship with President Lyndon Johnson and chaired the Rules Committee of the 1964 Democratic National Convention. In 1970, having been out of state government and elective office for four years, he ran for Governor again, but he was defeated by State Senator Jimmy Carter in a contentious and hard-fought campaign.

After leaving the Governor’s office in 1967, Sanders founded the law firm now known as Troutman Sanders LLP, which has grown into an international firm with more than 600 attorneys. Sanders managed the firm for 25 years and continued to serve the firm as Chairman Emeritus and as a partner – who continued to come to the office most days until his death.

His career in business included service as Chairman of the Board of Directors of the First Georgia Bank, and service on the boards of directors of First Railroad and Banking Corporation, Fuqua Industries Inc., Cousins Mortgage & Equity Investors, Healthdyne Technologies and Matria Health Care, Inc.

Sanders was a member of the Augusta National Golf Club, Peachtree Golf Club and Piedmont Driving Club. He also served on the Atlanta Committee for the Olympic Games, and in 1997, he was inducted into the Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame. For much of his life he was active in the YMCA and was a long time member of the Board of Directors of the YMCA of Metropolitan Atlanta. He also was a long time member of the Second - Ponce de Leon Baptist Church.

Governor Sanders is survived by his wife of 67 years, Betty; his daughter, Betty Foy Botts, and son-in-law, R. David Botts of Atlanta; his son, Carl Sanders, Jr., and daughter-in-law Christy Sanders. He also is survived by five grandchildren: Michael David Botts, Alyssa Betty Foy Botts, Caroline Sanders Hamburg

(together with her husband Billy Hamburg and children William Adam Hamburg and Montgomery Cate Hamburg), Keaton Marie Sanders, and Carl Sanders, III. He was preceded in death by grandson Austin Sanders Botts. The family is deeply grateful to all of those who have provided invaluable personal assistance to Governor Sanders, especially Willie Derrico, Margie Sims, Joanne Duffy, Jasmine Hammond, Janet Persaud, Craig Phillips, and his long-time Executive Assistant at Troutman Sanders, Doris Barnes.

Following a private burial in Augusta Georgia earlier in the week, a memorial service honoring Governor Sanders is scheduled for Saturday, November 22, 2014 at 11 o’clock at Second - Ponce de Leon Baptist Church. The family has designated the YMCA of Metro Atlanta or the University of Georgia School of Law for those wishing to make memorial donations in memory of Governor Sanders.

Pastor Dock Hollingsworth: “How do we understand God in the midst of crisis and suffering and fear?”
====================================================================================================

![Image 5](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/wp-content/plugins/innoscale-utility/assets/img/popular.png?post=587701&category=340219)For our 21st Century Plague project, we spoke with 17 Georgians about the toll of COVID-19.

By

[Steve Fennessy](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/author/steve-fennessy/ "Posts by Steve Fennessy")

\-

March 29, 2020

2848

_[For our 21st Century Plague project](https://www.atlantamagazine.com/great-reads/21st-century-plague/), we spoke with 17 Georgians about the toll of COVID-19. Below, Dock Hollingsworth—senior pastor Second-Ponce de Leon Baptist Church—describes the how the virus has impacted funeral services and the role of existential hope. (_Hollingsworth was interviewed on March 17)_  
_

Wednesday, March 11, was a turning point. We were here for the Wednesday night services. There was still a lot of levity. A 94-year-old man came up to me and said, “Boy, I was relieved that this is targeting people 60 to 80 since it’s been so long since I was 80.” By Thursday morning we were in a whole different mode. I was in a peer group with other Atlanta pastors. Everyone was asking, “Who’s cancelling Sunday? What measures are you taking?”

How do you keep a ministry going when touch is forbidden? How do we check on the shut-ins? How do I appropriately respond? We don’t have a rulebook for this.

For the first time today, somebody said, “We’re making all these plans as if none of us is going to get this virus.” The probability is, if it doesn’t enter our staff it will enter our church community.

Every industry has something peculiar that they’re facing. How do we do funerals and memorial services? If we do have a death in our community, it’s our practice to come together as a community and tell the stories. We can’t do that. An interment can’t wait. The staff here will do small graveside services and we’ll encourage families to push a memorial service into the future.

We are in the holy season of Lent right now. It’s already designed to be a season of introspection and asking the big questions. So in many ways this makes the Lenten questions more real and more pressing because the ground is shaky under people. But personally the ground doesn’t feel that shaky to me. Because I have a different kind of existential hope. We may see people turning to the church to ask, _Are there answers there that perhaps I’ve been making fun of for a long time?_ This is an opportunity to live inside a hope that is not built on markets, or how many widgets you can sell.

This Sunday \[March 22\] we’re doing a livestream of the service, and I do have to speak a pastoral word into this anxiety. So I’m trying to figure out that now. What do you say that’s pastoral and hopeful and grounded in reality?

How do we understand God in the midst of crisis and suffering and fear? A theology that moves into loving action is a wholesome theology. I’ve actually experienced less fear \[in conversation with members\] and more conversations about what kind of opportunity this is to be a loving witness and agent of God’s love in the world. Two women who stopped me yesterday who said, “We’re cooped up in the house so please tell us which of our older church members need grocery runs or pharmacy runs.” That’s what I mean.

_You can watch the sermon Hollingsworth gave on March 22_ [_here_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0QV0RAfBzzU)_; it begins at the 18-minute mark._

Second-Ponce de Leon Welcomes Dock Hollingsworth as New Senior Pastor
=====================================================================

###### 

[**Lisa Jones**,](https://patch.com/users/l-jones-56d60139) Neighbor

Posted Wed, Sep 11, 2013 at 10:09 am ET

![Image 4](https://patch.com/img/cdn/users/2350881/2013/09/raw/b8777cf3f5c11298a06c8ccf96a75fd9.gif)

Second-Ponce de Leon Baptist Church in Buckhead recently voted unanimously to call Dr. James Neil (Dock) Hollingsworth, Jr. as its seventh pastor. Hollingsworth’s first Sunday in the pulpit of the 159-year-old Peachtree Road church will be Sept. 22 at 11 a.m.

When Hollingsworth came to Second-Ponce de Leon as interim preacher 15 months ago, he did not anticipate eventually serving as senior pastor. He had served as interim pastor at nine different congregations over the past 12 years.

Hollingsworth also worked at Mercer University’s Macon and Atlanta campuses for the past 18 years. He was Assistant Dean and Assistant Professor of Leadership and Supervised Ministry at Mercer University’s McAfee School of Theology. He was also Executive Director for The Center for Teaching Churches. Prior to his time at Mercer, Hollingsworth served in churches in North Carolina and Georgia.

Find out what's happening in Buckheadfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Subscribe

“I fully thought I would retire at McAfee but the energy and possibility of this place has captured my imagination, and by God’s grace it would not let me go,” said Hollingsworth of Second-Ponce de Leon.

As a teen growing up in the Atlanta area, Hollingsworth attended special events at Second-Ponce de Leon with his high school friends. While at Mercer University for his undergraduate work, several of his college friends attended Second-Ponce de Leon. Hollingsworth received his M. Div. degree from The Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary in Wake Forest, N.C. In 2008, he completed the DMin program at McAfee.

Find out what's happening in Buckheadfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Subscribe

Hollingsworth serves on the board of the Lord’s Day Alliance of North America and The Care and Counseling Center of Georgia. He and his wife of 29 years, Melissa, are the parents of adult twins. Their daughter, Haley, is married to Chris Clement and they live in Chicago. Their son, Brendan, works with Marriott in Macon.

Second-Ponce de Leon worship services are held at 11 a.m. on Sundays in the Sanctuary. The church engages in community outreach through hands-on missions work, a fitness facility and a preschool. For additional information, visit the Second-Ponce de Leon Web site at [www.spdl.org](http://www.spdl.org/).

##### From the
### **Pastor Search Committee**

Welcome to Second-Ponce!


We are a family of Christian believers on the brink of newness in the life of our congregation ... new joys,
new ideas, new faces and new opportunities to serve God and our community. Admittedly, we’re in a
space that fills us with possibility, but we also have a sense of uncertainty. Change is never easy, but we
are ready to stretch ourselves and explore new methods to reach our community for Christ.


**How It Started**


After more than a decade of service, our previous Senior Pastor shared a desire to simplify his ministry
and transition to a smaller congregation, a change that would support a slower pace in the next phase of
life. The anxiety of this news was heightened by the departure of our Associate Pastor who accepted a
senior pastorate of his own only a few months earlier. In spite of the upheaval, and thanks to our
courageous and dedicated staff and leadership, we soon got to work seizing the opportunity to set a new
course for Second-Ponce.


**What Happened Next**


As a congregation, our first steps forward were a series of deliberate and strategic actions to fill ministry
gaps and begin the search process. The Executive Committee of the Deacons was tasked with finding an
Interim Senior Pastor and the church body confirmed a Pastor Search Committee. As that committee,
we led the congregation through an assessment process of surveys and listening sessions and then began
crafting a profile of our church and its future leader. What you are about to read is the fruit of that work.


**Where We Are Now**


We are in the process of accepting resumes, evaluating credentials and having conversations about
potential candidates. Calling a new Senior Pastor is a commitment that will define how Second-Ponce
participates in the eternal family of God. And so here we are ... mindful of the road but enjoying the
journey.


Before reading further, know that we have prayed for you as a possible candidate to lead our church. We
ask that you pray for us as we seek God’s will.


In Hopeful Prayer,

The Second-Ponce Pastor Search Committee



1


**We’re the Pastor Search Committee**

leadership to read our church profile and consider a future at SecondPonce. To apply for our Senior Pastor position, upload a letter of
[introduction and your resume on our website. Your participation and](http://www.spdl.org/pastorsearch)

information will remain confidential.

#### OUR COMMUNITY Community History

**Built on Relationships**


Modern-day Second-Ponce was formed when three Buckhead churches merged. The first, Second Baptist
Church, was founded in 1854. During the Civil War, it was spared from being burned due to the efforts of
Father Thomas O’Reilly who was the Catholic priest at the nearby Immaculate Conception Church. In
1929, the second and third founding churches, Ponce de Leon Avenue Baptist and Buckhead Baptist,
merged and moved to the corner of Peachtree and East Wesley Roads where SPdL sits today. Three years
later, on November 18, 1932, the merger of Second Baptist with Ponce de Leon Baptist Church birthed
Second-Ponce.


**Ministry Milestones**


In the last 93 years, we have experienced milestones that remain threads in our
church tapestry. Below, we’ve shared a few highlights from ministry areas that remain
priorities for Second-Ponce. Scan or click this code to see more landmark occasions

in the life of our church.


**Scan or Click**



**Using Technology for Ministry Growth**


In the 1930's, soon after our formation, we
began a radio broadcasting ministry. In 1962,
our first worship service telecast premiered.
Today, our TV ministry continues and has
expanded to livestreaming on multiple
platforms.


**Working Toward Racial Reconciliation**


In 2018, we curated a 4-part series, “Use Me,
God,” about the intersection of race and faith.
The event marked the 50th anniversary of the
assassination of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King,
Jr. Speakers included Ambassador Andrew
Young and author Taylor Branch.



![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11249949808413089541/11249949808413089541.pdf-4-0.png)

**Supporting Churches & Church Starts**


Since 1951, SPdL has started churches and
fnancially supported the creation of new
congregations across Atlanta. Recently, we
increased our geographical footprint in this
area by supporting a church in Blairsville,
Georgia, nearly two hours outside of Atlanta.


**Bridging Gaps in Community Services**


In 2022, we partnered with the Cathedral of
Christ the King to create a new preschool,
CTK Preschool at Second-Ponce. The school,
operating from our campus, continues to
exceed enrollment expectations.



3


#### OUR COMMUNITY Geographical Community

**Opportunities for Growth & Ministry**


The majority of those who work in
Buckhead commute into the area from

other parts of Atlanta, but the
combination of high-rise complexes,
single-family homes and senior living
facilities make for a growing population
of residents. Buckhead’s growth rate is
2.34%, outpacing Atlanta’s rate of
1.38%. The latest census data shows the

biggest growth demographic in the area
is single adults aged 20–40. There are
8 schools (including a Title One school)
in our 30305-zip code and 6 university
campuses within a short distance.

#### OUR COMMUNITY Campus Community

The location and size of our church campus allow us to open our doors to the community by hosting events
and renting office space to other organizations. Meet our current tenants. We’re proud to have them as
part of the Second-Ponce campus community.


**[Alma Domestic Violence Foundation](https://almadvf.org/)**


Alma provides direct services and training to sufferers and survivors of domestic violence
including financial literacy, healthcare and social services. They also work directly with
students regarding violence education and prevention in dating relationships.


**[Atlanta Suzuki Violin](https://atlantasuzukiviolin.com/)**


In 1991, violin instructor Virginia Sloan founded Atlanta Suzuki Violin–a specific training method for teaching
violin in early childhood. She incorporates a wealth of performing experience training and her love for children
into her approach.


**[Christ the King Preschool at Second-Ponce](https://www.ctkpreschoolat2p.com/)**

Christ the King Preschool at Second-Ponce provides half-day programs to students aged

**[Collective Learning Academy](https://www.claoa.com/)**

The Collective Learning Academy (CLA) educates and empowers students with disabilities
so they can live, learn and lead. The mission of CLA is to maximize the potential of each
student, meeting them at their current academic and functional level.


**[Respite Care Atlanta](https://www.respitecareatlanta.org/)**

Respite Care Atlanta (RCA) provides spiritually integrated respite care for adults
with cognitive challenges and support for their caregivers. SPdL is one of the

#### SPdL DISTINCTIVES Mission & Vision

**Our Mission**


Experiencing community by welcoming the stranger and
caring for our neighbor as Christ did.


**Growing in Christ and community—sharing God’s love in the world.**



![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11249949808413089541/11249949808413089541.pdf-8-0.png)

into daily practice.


**Core Values**



Embodying Christ’s love through
opportunities to make broken places

whole.



These are the principles to which we hold ourselves accountable in living out our mission.


**Community**


We believe God wants us to build genuine community and care for one another. We
welcome the stranger into our hearts and lives as God has welcomed us in Christ.


**Discipleship**


We are committed to investing in others by equipping people to discover and implement
God’s call for their lives.


**Missions**

generosity because God has been so generous to us in Jesus.

#### SPdL DISTINCTIVES Beliefs & Practices

**Baptist Beliefs**


We believe that the Holy Spirit empowers local churches to share the Good News of Jesus Christ. To
that end, we value the “four fragile freedoms” as defined by Baptist historian Walter B. Shurden.


**Bible Freedom** Baptists believe that the Bible is a foundational record of God’s revelation to
humankind. Both individuals and congregations are free to read and interpret the
Bible under the Lordship of Christ and the leadership of the Holy Spirit. Baptists are
not beholden to any creeds or reliant on mediators outside of Scripture.



**Soul Freedom**


**Church Freedom**


**Religious Freedom**


**Christian Practices**



Soul freedom affirms that each person is created in the image of God and is therefore
able and responsible—not by force or coercion from a doctrine, clergy or the
government—for their own direct relationship with God. Baptists believe people may
only come to Christ on their own volition. Soul freedom is sometimes called the
“Priesthood of Believers.”


Church Freedom (or the autonomy of the local church) is the historic belief that local
churches are free, under the Lordship of Jesus, to determine their membership and
leadership, to order their worship and work, to ordain whomever they perceive to be
gifted for ministry (regardless of gender) and to participate in the larger Body of
Christ (other churches and other denominations).


Religious freedom is the historic Baptist affirmation of freedom OF religion, freedom
FOR religion, and freedom FROM religion. The earliest Baptists championed the
separation of church and state in the American colonies and, later, the United States.
Churches and individuals should be free to worship in whatever manner they choose
and with whomever they choose. All people, no matter their religious background,
should be free from any coercion to worship, and free from the intervention of the
state in matters of religion.



**Baptism:** As Baptists, we participate in and perform “believer’s baptism” which means individuals who have

made a personal decision to follow Jesus are baptized. Our practice is full immersion in water, symbolizing
the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. While baptism is important as a public declaration of faith,
Baptists do not believe it is necessary for salvation.


**The Lord’s Supper:** In Baptist tradition, the Lord’s Supper, or Communion, refers to a symbolic act of worship
where followers of Christ partake of bread and cup to remember Jesus' death on the cross through the
symbolism of his broken body and spilled blood. Communion unites us as one body in Christ’s commission
to continue His ministry. At Second-Ponce, we invite anyone who claims Jesus Christ as their Lord and
Savior to participate in this ritual.

**Missions**


Second-Ponce continues a faithful commitment to missions through financial support

Financial Support: Because of our endowments, SPdL can do far more than most

#### SPdL MINISTRIES Other Ministry Initiatives

**Benevolence**


In addition to our long-term missions commitments, we maintain supplies for those who come to SecondPonce with immediate needs. Meal and Metro bus cards, snack packs, bottled water and clothing are
given out as needed along with information about accessing long-term assistance.


**Community Wellness Center**


The Community Wellness Center at Second-Ponce provides a neighborhood space
for those seeking wellness of the mind, body and spirit. While this is a ministry of
our church, it is also a full-service gym offering top quality fitness equipment,
programs and classes. CWC membership rates are lower than most other facilities
in the community and Second-Ponce members receive a discount.

![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11249949808413089541/11249949808413089541.pdf-12-0.png)

#### ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE Governing Bodies

**Board of Deacons**


Consistent with New Testament Scripture, Deacons are to be ministers and servants of the church
providing spiritual leadership, care and support for the congregation. A new class of Deacons is elected
annually by the congregation, and our current Deacon body is made up of 22 men and women serving 3year terms as well as 12 Life Deacons. The Executive Committee of the Board of Deacons has authority
to act on behalf of the full body on matters requiring action between regularly scheduled meetings. The
Executive Committee is composed of seven members: the Senior Pastor, Deacon Chair, Deacon ViceChair, Immediate Past Chair and three at-large members.


**Personnel Committee**


The Personnel Committee provides advice, support and guidance to the Senior Pastor, ministerial staff
and Deacon Executive Committee on matters related to church employees. They also set guidelines
and maintain oversight in matters such as staffing, compensation and disciplinary actions.


**Standing Committees**


Standing Committees are groups charged with responsibility for a particular task pertaining to the
operation of the church. This includes special committees required by the church bylaws and others
determined to be necessary by the Board of Deacons. Membership of the standing committees is to be
determined by the Board of Deacons. The Senior Pastor and Deacon Chair serve as ex-officio members
of all standing committees. Church staff members may serve in an advisory capacity. Current standing
committees are Executive, Facilities, Finance, Nominating, Personnel and Planned Gifts.


**Ministry & Leadership Councils**


Second-Ponce's lay ministry leadership is organized around four Ministry Councils: Community,
Discipleship, Missions and Worship. These councils correspond to Second-Ponce's four core values and
are overseen by the Deacon Board. Service teams and other programs fall under each of the councils,
and councils may establish teams/groups to do work on an on-going or ad-hoc basis. The Leadership
Council brings together the ministers and lay leadership to ensure that all the ministry efforts of the
church are coordinated and aligned. The Leadership Council includes the Senior Pastor, Deacon Chair,
Ministerial Staff, Church Administrator, the chairs of each Ministry Council and the chairs of key

committees.

**Senior Pastor Position Description | Second-Ponce de Leon Baptist Church**


**Overview:** The Senior Pastor is the spiritual and administrative leader of the church. He or She is


responsible for proclaiming the gospel of Jesus Christ; teaching Biblical truths through challenging


sermons; engaging in pastoral care ministries both within the church and the community; facilitating


outreach efforts to new congregants; and for leading collaborative opportunities to grow the church


through finances and attendance.


**Status:** Full-time position with a competitive salary, 403(b) retirement contributions, health


insurance, long term disability coverage and housing allowance. Additional package benefits include:


  Paid time off including sick leave and a vacation fund


  - Sabbatical leave


  - Relocation allowances


  Professional development and continuing education support


Organizational Relationships:


  - _Supervised By_ : Personnel Committee


  _Supervisory Responsibilities_ : All Church Staff (Direct Supervision: Ministerial Staff,


Administrator)


  - _Staff Teams_ : Ministerial Staff


  _Congregational Teams_ : Executive Committee and Leadership Council, Ex-officio member of


committees


**Essential Job Functions:**


**1.** **Pastoral Leadership**


    Inspire spiritual growth of the congregation through Biblically based sermons, dynamic,


Spirit-led worship services and observance of ordinances and Bible teaching. Responsible


for pulpit supply when away.


    Provide vision, leadership, planning and evaluation for the coordinated work of the


church.


    Lead the church in effective programs of Bible study, discipleship, evangelism, outreach,


new member assimilation, leadership development and community ministries.


  Encourage and model congregational support of local, state, national and international


missions through the giving of time, talent, finances and resources.


  Provide pastoral care through prayer, visitation, funerals, weddings, baby dedications and


spiritual counseling.


  Conduct wedding ceremonies, funeral services and other life rites of passage events as


needed with the prerogative of delegating to other staff members when appropriate.


  Challenge the church to faithful stewardship and ensure the proper use of offerings and


income.


  Represent Second-Ponce through community involvement.


  Cooperate with other ministry partners in matters of mutual interest and concern.


  Prepare an annual strategic plan in collaboration with the Leadership Council that


includes goals with measurable outcomes as appropriate.


  Promote harmony within the staff and members of the congregation.


  Cooperate with the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship global office and the Cooperative


Baptist Fellowship of Georgia, unless the church directs otherwise.


**2.** **Administrative Leadership**


  Lead and oversee the ministerial staff, coordinate and motivate committees and councils,


inspire Deacons and volunteers to serve.


  Be knowledgeable of and adhere to church bylaws and personnel policies and procedures.


  Serve ex-officio on all standing boards, committees and councils with the prerogative of


delegating to other ministerial staff.


  Perform other duties that the Personnel Committee and Senior Pastor may agree upon.


  Recommends, in consultation with the Personnel Committee, additional staff positions


and salary adjustments as deemed necessary to accomplish the church mission.


**3.** **Core Competencies**


  - _Heart_ : A heart to serve the Lord and a vibrant relationship with Jesus Christ.


  _Trust & Integrity_ : Acts and speaks in ways that are direct and truthful; keeps confidence;


admits mistakes; is accountable in their commitments; adheres to high ethical standards


as well as the core values of the church.


- _Interpersonal Relationships_ : Interacts well with others; builds constructive relationships;


demonstrates effective communication skills; gives and receives candid feedback; is open


to different viewpoints; uses diplomacy and tact; willing to work in a team context when


needed.


_Respectful_ : Values diverse perspectives; shows sensitivity to individual differences; treats


others fairly and with respect; seeks and considers diverse perspectives and ideas.


_Flexibility & Change_ : Understands the dynamics of change and the need to build


consensus during decision making endeavors; able to adapt to the varying needs of those


served.


_Managing Purpose & Vision_ : Understands the culture and values of this church; articulates


and supports its mission and direction; communicates a compelling and inspired sense of


how individuals contribute to the church’s purpose and vision.


_Conflict Management_ : Steps up to conflicts, seeing them as opportunities; addresses


conflicts by focusing on the issues at hand to develop effective solutions when disputes or


disagreements occur; helps others resolve conflicts by providing impartial mediation


when needed.


- _Communication_ : Writes and speaks effectively; demonstrates openness and honesty;


listens well during meetings and feedback sessions; explains reasoning behind own


opinions; asks others for their opinions; engages stakeholders at the appropriate level of


decision making; uses consideration and tact when offering opinions; embraces digital


technology.


- _Executive Leadership_ : Has the willingness and ability to focus on the larger view of the


church rather than one’s own area of functional or operational responsibility; can think,


reflect, conceptualize and converse on issues of strategic significance to the church's


future.


_Biblical Scholarship_ : Keeps studying and learning to gain deeper understanding of


Scripture; delves into Biblical interpretation, life application and holistic implementation.
